rationale: A wins by a nose because it recognizes there is a real consumer-health story hiding under the trade fight: "Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs now have a cheaper option — with an FDA warning attached." B is cleaner on sourcing, but it kills that same avenue as "Patients priced out of branded semaglutide finally have an option" — `hallucinated_fact`, which is too severe for an angle that can be made honest with price and patient proof. Both sets understand the FDA/manufacturer conflict; A gives the founder one more usable door and the correct next move, while B sends them back to "newsjack-detector" like the story has not already arrived.
gaps_in_A: "branded drugmakers want it stopped" overstates the supplied fact. Pushback is not the same as demanding the launch be stopped.
"Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs" leans past the fact block. The cheaper-price fact supports an access angle, but the actual patient hardship needs a named patient or price proof.
"telehealth moves from writing prescriptions to running diagnostics" is a little grand for one at-home lab-testing service. If the test is optional, that headline collapses fast.
"Its next act is a regulatory-exposed bet" is directionally right, but it needs disclosed growth exposure before it becomes more than a smart investor question.
gaps_in_B: "Patients priced out of branded semaglutide finally have an option" was refused too aggressively. Lack of price and patient proof makes it conditional, not dead.
"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is the wrong handoff. The launch fact is already here; the next move is proof gathering and journalist fit-checking.
"If either is live this week, the first two angles move from week to 4hr" treats the FDA/manufacturer facts as if they must be fresh pegs. The launch itself is a valid now hook.
The kept set misses a mainstream consumer-health frame. It has trade, regulatory, care-model, and markets angles, but leaves the patient access/risk story on the floor.
